frameworks.name: The Four Functions of Business
frameworks.definition: Every business requires four specialized roles: marketer (promotion and brand), salesperson (conversion), product person (design and experience), and operator/customer success (implementation and retention).

frameworks.name: Three Levels of Entrepreneurial Evolution
frameworks.definition: Players progress from individual contributor (doing the work), to specialist/executive (managing a function), to coach (recruiting, building culture, and delegating decisions).

frameworks.name: Output Formula
frameworks.definition: Total output is determined by two variables: volume of activity (hours of work) multiplied by leverage of activity (impact per unit of work).

claims.text: Hard work alone does not determine wealth. Warren Buffett, by his own account, reads 5-6 hours per day, eats McDonald's, and makes a couple good decisions per year, yet generates vastly more wealth than people who claim no one can outwork them.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Work output is dictated not by hours invested but by the leverage of the decisions made within those hours.

claims.text: Every person has 24 hours in a day. Claiming no one can outwork you is mathematically false if your claim rests on hours worked, because anyone working the same hours per day would be equally hard-working. The competitive advantage must come from something other than volume of activity.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Hours are a finite, equally distributed resource; competitive advantage requires lever selection, not lever-agnostic volume.

anchors.region: any person working full available hours

claims.text: When a CEO at Acquisition.com joins, they work virtually every hour of every day. The only lever for growth beyond maximum work hours is replacing low-leverage activities with high-leverage activities. The lever is not more work; it is better work.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Once a person maximizes hours worked, the only way to increase output is to redirect time from low-leverage activities to high-leverage ones, identified by analyzing calendars and org charts.
bounded_by: Does not apply when a founder has not yet maximized work hours

claims.text: To identify which activities should be delegated or eliminated, examine what the founder spends time on and determine which activities lack leverage. If a large percentage of activities are of a certain low-leverage type and no one in the org chart already owns them, that indicates a new role to hire.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Systematic analysis of time allocation reveals structural role gaps that, when filled, create output multipliers.

claims.text: The "no one can outwork me" mentality misidentifies the source of competitive advantage. The claim should instead be about recruitment, culture building, and team leverage: "No one can be out-recruited by me," "No one can build a culture like me," or "No one can lead like me."
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: High-leverage activities (recruiting, culture, leadership) create organization-wide multipliers; effort-intensive activities (personal work volume) do not compound across the team.

claims.text: Winning at the highest levels of business is about team composition and role fit, not individual work ethic. A team with complementary specialized roles (marketer, salesperson, product person, operator) beats a team where every member tries to do everything, just as a battle party with a healer, mage, and paladin beats a party of 10 paladins.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Business at scale where multiple roles can be distributed
claims.mechanism: Role specialization allows each person to maximize their comparative advantage. Diversity of skills creates resilience and coverage of all required functions.
bounded_by: Does not apply to very early stage (single founder bootstrapping)
Does not apply to roles that genuinely cannot be split

claims.text: Business functions are not interchangeable. A brilliant marketer can be a poor salesperson, and a good salesperson can be a poor marketer. The four core functions—marketing (building brand and making things known), sales (converting attention), product (design and customer experience), and operations (retention and customer success)—require different skill sets and should not be assumed to coexist in one person.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Marketing and sales are distinct conversion funnels with different success metrics and psychological drivers; conflating them causes optimization failures.

claims.text: As an enterprise scales, each role requires deeper specialization and more experienced people. A CEO at Shopify is not the same person as the head of product; they are fulfilling different functions that require different expertise and operational focus.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Each function's complexity grows with scale; generalists become bottlenecks; specialization enables exponential growth.

claims.text: The progression of an entrepreneur is: (1) player—doing the work yourself; (2) specialist/executive—managing a function (CMO, chief sales officer, chief product officer); (3) coach—recruiting top talent, building culture, and solving the next problem.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Each level compounds the previous one. A player who does not evolve to coach cannot build systems that outlast them.

claims.text: The primary job of a CEO at the coach level is to have the highest return on time of anyone in the organization. Every hour a CEO spends must be replaced with an activity that builds the business even more, ensuring their time stays in the highest-leverage category.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Role is CEO or executive coach
claims.mechanism: As the CEO delegates and scales, their time becomes the most scarce resource. Continued leverage requires always solving the next problem, not the current one.

claims.text: The value created by a CEO is measured as the delta between what the organization would achieve without them and what it achieves with them. A CEO who can turn around a business (even a large one) in 2-3 years by setting standards and modeling values creates exponential leverage across the entire organization.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: CEO has authority to set culture and standards
claims.mechanism: Leadership leverages through modeling. Standards and values propagate, multiplying across all team members' daily decisions.

claims.text: Best coaches recruit continuously and create a farm system underneath the top-level team, ensuring that the organization can sustain competitive advantage by always having high-performing talent ready to step into roles. This differs sharply from building a "star player" organization around a single founder.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Continuous recruitment creates organizational immunity to talent loss and ensures sustained improvement every year.

claims.text: The output formula is: Volume of Activity multiplied by Leverage of Activity equals Total Output. Early-stage founders maximize volume (doing more activities), but this quickly hits capacity. The only uncapped lever is to increase the leverage of each activity, which requires delegation and systematization.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Volume is bounded by hours in a day. Leverage is unbounded because systems can be replicated across multiple people.

anchors.value: growth limited by personal activity volume
growth limited by activity leverage; volume is maxed
growth limited by delegation depth and team leverage

claims.text: Metrics like waking up early, going to bed late, or not sleeping a lot are superstitions about success, not actual drivers of it. These are activity-volume proxies, not leverage. They become irrelevant once volume is maximized, and they distract from the actual lever: leverage.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Superstition about work hours persists because early-stage founders do benefit from more volume; the correlation is misidentified as causation at scale.
bounded_by: Does not apply to founders who have not yet maximized basic activity volume

claims.text: If you cannot "get your ass off the couch" to do the work, then the starting point is to maximize activity volume. But once you have exhausted that capacity, the only lever left is leverage of activity.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Discipline to execute on volume precedes the sophistication to recognize leverage. The two stages are sequential, not simultaneous.
bounded_by: Does not apply to founders already working at or near capacity

examples.text: Warren Buffett exemplifies the leverage-over-volume principle. He reads 5-6 hours per day, eats McDonald's for lunch every day, and makes a couple of good decisions per year. Despite doing far fewer activities than most entrepreneurs, he generates vastly more wealth because each decision carries enormous leverage. His calendar does not look like a hard-working person's calendar; it looks like a person playing a different game.

When a CEO from Acquisition.com joins Hormozi's operation, they are already working virtually every hour of every day. The coaching intervention is not to make them work more. Instead, Hormozi and his team analyze the CEO's calendar and org chart, identify which activities lack leverage (and thus can be delegated or eliminated), and redirect those hours into high-leverage activities. The total hours worked does not increase; the composition of activities shifts radically.

A typical all-star team with superior supporting cast will be beaten by a well-coordinated team with a less-famous star. The difference is not in the talent of the star but in how the team functions together. Similarly, companies with a founder-as-superstar model are outcompeted by companies like Apple that distribute expertise across specialized roles and make the organization stronger than any individual.

Shopify's founder stepped away from the CEO role to become head of product, a high-leverage position that plays to his strengths. This is a deliberate move away from the "founder must do everything" model and toward the "founder finds their best role and recruits others to fill the rest" model. The organization's strength comes from having a product visionary (the founder) and a professional CEO managing all other functions.

At Acquisition.com, Hormozi looks at what a new CEO spends time on. He discovers they're spending a large percentage of their week on a certain low-leverage activity—say, operational administration or customer success details that could be delegated. Since no one in the org chart owns customer success at scale, Hormozi's recommendation is to hire a chief customer success officer. This single hire frees the CEO to focus on strategy and business development, two orders of magnitude higher leverage.

practices.text: Analyze your calendar and org chart to identify which activities you spend time on and which lack leverage. For any large cluster of low-leverage activities not owned by anyone on the org chart, create a new role and hire someone.

Do not claim or celebrate hard work as your competitive advantage. Instead, claim excellence in recruitment, culture building, team leverage, and leadership. These create compounding returns across the organization.

Recruit people with complementary skills, not clones of yourself. Identify the core functions your business needs (marketing, sales, product, operations) and hire specialists for each, not generalists who try to do everything.
As CEO, every hour spent must be replaced with an activity that builds the business even more. Continuously identify the next bottleneck and solve it, rather than optimizing existing operations.
Build a farm system of talent underneath the executive team so that you can always promote from within and never be dependent on external recruiting. This creates sustained competitive advantage.
